name: Go
summary: A small, statically typed language from Google that compiles in seconds to one static binary, with goroutines, channels and a garbage collector built in.
intro: Go compiles ahead of time to machine code. The standard `gc` toolchain links statically by default, so a program ships as one file that carries the Go runtime with it: the scheduler, the garbage collector and the type information needed for reflection and panic stack traces. Setting `GOOS` and `GOARCH` picks the target, so building a Linux ARM binary on a Mac is one environment variable away. Unused imports are a compile error, not a warning, which keeps dependency graphs honest and builds fast.

Concurrency is in the language. `go f()` starts a goroutine, a function that the runtime multiplexes onto a small pool of operating system threads; a new goroutine gets a stack of a few kilobytes that grows and shrinks as needed, so hundreds of thousands can run in one process. Goroutines talk over typed channels, an idea taken from Tony Hoare’s Communicating Sequential Processes, summed up in the Go proverb “Do not communicate by sharing memory. Instead, share memory by communicating.” Memory is managed by a concurrent, non-moving mark-and-sweep garbage collector whose pauses are often under a millisecond. Since Go 1 in 2012, code written for an older 1.x release is promised to keep compiling; generics arrived in Go 1.18 (March 2022), and the latest releases are Go 1.26 (February 2026) and Go 1.27 (August 2026).
strengths: Fast builds and one statically linked binary per program, so a deploy can be a single file copy
Goroutines and channels make concurrent network servers straightforward, with a runtime that parks blocked goroutines for you
A small language with one formatting style (`gofmt`) and a strict compatibility promise since Go 1, so old code keeps compiling
Cross-compiling to another OS or CPU is built in: set `GOOS` and `GOARCH` and build
limits: A garbage collector and a runtime come with every binary, which costs memory and CPU time that C, C++, Rust or Zig programs don’t pay
Deliberately few features: no exceptions, no inheritance, and generics only since 1.18, so some code is more repetitive than in richer languages
Maps aren’t safe for concurrent writes, and channels don’t prevent data races; the race detector finds them only at run time
Calling C through `cgo` needs a C toolchain for every target, and `cgo` is off by default when cross-compiling, so mixed Go and C code loses the easy cross-builds

snippet.title: Three goroutines send results over a channel
source: func square(n int, results chan<- int) {
go square(n, results) // three goroutines run concurrently
sum += <-results // receiving blocks until a goroutine sends
fmt.Println("sum of squares:", sum) // sum of squares: 14

story: By 2007, Google’s servers were written mostly in C++ and Java, and building them had become slow. Rob Pike’s account of the time describes one major Google binary of about 2,000 source files (4.2 MB) that expanded, through repeated `#include`s, into more than 8 GB of compiler input, and took 45 minutes to build even on a distributed build system. Programmers who wanted to move fast were drifting to dynamic languages such as Python, giving up safety and speed.

On 21 September 2007, Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson started sketching a new language on a whiteboard. Thompson had a first compiler by January 2008, Ian Taylor started a GCC front end that May, and Russ Cox joined late that year. Google released Go as an open-source project on 10 November 2009, promising builds that “feel instantaneous” and code that “runs close to the speed of C”.
Go 1, in March 2012, froze the language and standard library under a compatibility promise. Go then became the language of much cloud infrastructure, including Docker, Kubernetes and Terraform.

choices.why: C++ headers made every build reread the same files thousands of times. In Go a package imports only what it uses, an unused import is a compile error, and compiled packages carry what their importers need, so builds stay fast as code grows.

choices.choice: Garbage collection, not manual memory management
choices.why: Freeing memory safely is the hardest part of concurrent code, because objects pass between threads. The designers judged that a modern collector could be cheap and low-latency enough for network servers, and that it makes interfaces simpler too.

choices.choice: Goroutines and channels in the language
choices.why: Borrowed from CSP via Newsqueak and Limbo: cheap goroutines on growable stacks let a server use one goroutine per connection, and the runtime moves others off a thread that blocks in a system call.

choices.choice: A small language and a stability promise
choices.why: Go 1 was a cleanup release that then froze, so “programs will continue to compile and run without change … on a time scale of years”; new features come slowly.
